questions.q: How does pruning differ fundamentally from quantization?
options: Pruning changes the model's architecture entirely; quantization never does
Pruning removes weights entirely; quantization keeps every weight but lowers its precision
Quantization removes weights; pruning only lowers their precision
They are two names for exactly the same technique
questions.explain: Quantization keeps every weight and reduces how many bits represent it. Pruning removes weights (or structural pieces of the model) entirely, betting that many contribute little to the output.

questions.q: Why doesn't unstructured pruning usually speed up inference on standard GPU kernels?
options: Because unstructured pruning is illegal to run on GPUs
Because a dense matrix-multiply kernel still checks every entry regardless of scattered zeros, so compute isn't actually reduced without specialized sparse kernels
Because unstructured pruning always reduces accuracy to zero
Because unstructured pruning can only be applied to CPUs
questions.explain: Scattered zeros from unstructured pruning still sit inside what a standard kernel treats as a dense matrix — the hardware checks every entry anyway, so the main savings are in storage/transfer size, not compute.

questions.q: What is N:M (e.g. 2:4) sparsity, and why does it matter for real speedups?
options: A naming convention with no actual hardware relevance
A fixed pattern (e.g. exactly 2 of every 4 contiguous weights zeroed) that matches dedicated sparse tensor cores on newer NVIDIA GPUs
A technique that only works for quantization, not pruning
A method that removes 100% of a model's weights
questions.explain: N:M sparsity imposes a regular, fixed pattern that dedicated sparse tensor cores (on Ampere and newer NVIDIA GPUs) can accelerate directly, unlike arbitrary scattered zeros.

questions.q: What does magnitude pruning use to decide which weights to remove?
options: Random selection with no criterion
The weight's position in the file, removing the last weights added
The absolute value of each weight — smallest-magnitude weights are removed first
Only weights in the first layer of the model
questions.explain: Magnitude pruning assumes weights with the smallest absolute value contribute least to the output, so those are the first candidates for removal.

questions.q: Why is pruning almost always followed by fine-tuning?
options: Fine-tuning is required to make the pruned model load at all
Removing weights is a harsher intervention than lowering their precision, so fine-tuning lets remaining weights adjust and recover lost accuracy
Fine-tuning is only needed for structured pruning, never unstructured
Fine-tuning replaces the need for any pruning criterion
questions.explain: Because pruning zeros out weights entirely rather than just lowering their precision, teams typically fine-tune afterward (often iteratively, pruning a bit, fine-tuning, and repeating) to recover accuracy.
